topic: Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago from the disc of dust and gas around the young Sun; the Moon formed soon after, probably from a giant impact.
Its history is divided into four eons: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic.
Life appeared before 3.5 billion years ago; photosynthesis filled the air with oxygen about 2.4 billion years ago, and complex animals spread from about 540 million years ago.
Five mass extinctions reshaped life; after the last, 66 million years ago, mammals spread, and our genus Homo appeared about 2.8 million years ago.

Eons: Geologists measure deep time in Ma (millions of years ago) and Ga (billions of years ago).
Earth's history is split into four eons: Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic and Phanerozoic.
Eons divide into eras, eras into periods, and periods into epochs.
Geologic time scale: The geologic time scale orders Earth's history by the layers of rock laid down in each interval.
The first four billion years (the Precambrian) take up almost 90% of Earth's history, but the record is sparse.
The Phanerozoic, the last 539 million years, is the eon of abundant visible fossils and is divided most finely.
Solar System formation: In the solar nebula hypothesis, the Sun and planets formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust.
The cloud held hydrogen and helium from the Big Bang (13.8 billion years ago) and heavier elements made in exploded stars.
About 4.6 billion years ago the cloud began to collapse, perhaps set off by a nearby supernova; Earth grew by accretion within a few tens of millions of years.
Hadean and Archean Eons: The Hadean began with Earth's formation; the oldest mineral grains (zircons) are 4.4 billion years old and the oldest rocks about 4.0 billion.
A Mars-sized body, Theia, probably struck the young Earth; the debris formed the Moon (the giant-impact hypothesis).
Oceans condensed early, and the first continents began to form in the Archean, which started 4.03 billion years ago.
Life arose by at least 3.5 billion years ago; competing theories include an RNA world, iron–sulfur metabolism and lipid membranes first.
All living things descend from a last universal common ancestor (LUCA).
Proterozoic Eon: The Proterozoic ran from 2.5 billion to 538.8 million years ago; cratons grew into continents of modern size.
Cyanobacteria's photosynthesis produced the Great Oxygenation Event, which made the atmosphere oxygen-rich.
Eukaryotes (cells with a nucleus) emerged, followed by multicellular life.
Severe 'Snowball Earth' glaciations covered much of the planet; after the last, about 600 million years ago, life evolved faster.
Supercontinents such as Columbia and Rodinia assembled and broke apart.
Tectonics, paleogeography and climate: The Phanerozoic (538.8 million years ago to now) has three eras: Paleozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic.
Continents gathered into the supercontinent Pangaea by about 300 million years ago, which then broke up into today's continents.
Climate swung between warm greenhouse periods and icehouse periods with polar ice caps.
Cambrian explosion: From about 538 million years ago, most major animal groups appear in the fossil record within a few tens of millions of years.
It was an adaptive radiation into niches left empty by the extinct Ediacaran organisms.
Animals with shells and skeletons, including trilobites, molluscs and the first vertebrates, appeared.
Colonization of land: Oxygen from photosynthesis built an ozone layer that blocked ultraviolet light, making land habitable.
Microbes may have reached land by 3 billion years ago; plants and fungi followed in the Ordovician and Silurian.
Arthropods were among the first animals to live on land.
Evolution of tetrapods: A mass extinction ended the Ordovician about 443 million years ago, perhaps due to an ice age.
About 380–375 million years ago, the first tetrapods evolved from lobe-finned fish; fins became limbs.
Amniotes, whose eggs survive on dry land, later split into synapsids (the mammal line) and sauropsids (reptiles and birds).
Extinctions: There have been five great mass extinctions: end-Ordovician, Late Devonian, end-Permian, end-Triassic and end-Cretaceous.
The end-Permian extinction, 252 million years ago, was the worst, killing about 90% of marine species.
The end-Cretaceous extinction, 66 million years ago, caused by an asteroid impact, wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.
Diversification of mammals: The first true mammals were small, probably nocturnal animals living alongside the dinosaurs from the late Triassic.
Mammals diversified rapidly only after the dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago.
Primates appeared early in the Cenozoic.
Human evolution: About 6 million years ago, a small African ape was the last common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees.
One branch soon walked upright; the first members of the genus Homo appeared by about 2 million years ago.
Farming began about 10,000 years ago, leading to cities, writing and the first civilisations.
